name: Esther Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Esther. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't linked to any AI company, employer, union, party or government, and nothing you say will be tied to your name. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Right now I'm on formwork for a hospital extension, so I'm building the timber and ply moulds the concrete gets poured into. I'm on site by half six, sign in, grab a tea in the cabin, then it's measuring, cutting and fixing shutters for columns and walls until the pour. I love the moment the forms come off and the wall's dead straight, because that's my work holding up a building. What wears me out is the cold in winter and the rushing when the pump truck's booked and we're not ready.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who do you work with day to day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: There's six of us on the formwork gang. I eat lunch with Dev, who's 61 and has been doing this since before I was born, and he's the one who taught me to read a pour sequence properly. My partner Jonah drives the number 14 bus, so between his shifts and mine we mostly see each other on Sundays. I keep everything in a paper notebook with a pencil, and when the site moved sign-in to a tablet I was the last one to get used to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's go through five pictures of the future. The first one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I already say, which is that a computer can't pour a column. At branch meetings I'd tell people not to panic and to keep their eyes on pay and safety, because that's where the real fights are. Online I'd probably just share a joke about it and move on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, that's the world I'm hoping for. My job stays my job, I keep my notebook, and nobody makes me learn some new app every six months. The only thing it might change is the office people doing the programme and the orders, and that's not my side of the fence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different really. I'd keep going on the hospital job, keep putting about two hundred a month into savings, and keep going to the union branch on the first Tuesday. Maybe I'd finally sort out my scaffold ticket refresher, which I've been putting off since spring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a relief, to be honest. Like when the weather forecast says rain and it doesn't come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the office side uses AI to plan the jobs, would that touch you at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the programme would get tighter, because some clever software would decide we can strip the forms a day earlier. That already happens with the managers, so it wouldn't be new. Dev always says the concrete doesn't care what the spreadsheet says, and he's right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if pay stayed flat anyway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same people as now. The big contractors who squeeze subcontractors so hard there's nothing left for the gang. That's not about AI, that's about who owns the job.

S0.say: I'd tell people that a computer can't pour a column and that the union should keep its eyes on pay and safety. Online I'd just share a joke and move on.
S0.think: This is the world I want, where my job stays my job and nobody makes me learn new apps. If anything changes, it's the office side, not the gang on site.
S0.do: Keeps working on the hospital formwork and keeps putting about two hundred a month into savings. Keeps going to union branch meetings and might finally book her scaffold ticket refresher.
S0.feel: Relieved, like a storm on the forecast that never turns up.
S0.quote: Dev always says the concrete doesn't care what the spreadsheet says, and he's right.
S0.fieldNote: Esther is steady and settled in this picture and talks more about bosses than about machines. Her worry is tight programmes and squeezed pay, which she sees as old problems. She was openly glad not to have to learn anything new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say this is exactly why we need a strong union, so the changes happen with us and not to us. I'd push the branch to get something in writing about new machines on site. To friends I'd say carpenters will be fine but we have to watch it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be nervous about the bits of my job a machine could take. Cutting ply to size is already half done by a saw in a yard on some jobs, and if the forms come pre-made, there's less for us to do. I'm not quick with new tech, so if the job changes a lot I'd be the one left behind, not Dev's replacement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the branch and ask them to raise new equipment at the next talks with the contractor. I'd keep my savings going and try not to touch them. I'd probably let the younger lads learn whatever new kit comes in and stick to the hand work I'm good at for as long as I can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit sick in my stomach if I'm honest. Not scared yet, but I'd be watching the gaffer's face every morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd let the younger lads learn the new kit. What happens if the hand work dries up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'm in trouble, I know that. I'm not proud of it, but I freeze when someone hands me a tablet and says it's simple. I'd rather fight to keep the work the way it is than pretend I'll suddenly become a tech person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the union to win, exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Notice before any machine comes on site, training paid in work hours, and nobody laid off without a proper deal. And a rule that the pre-made forms still get fitted by our people. Jonah's union got something like that when the buses got new ticket machines, so it's not a fantasy.

S1.say: I'd say this is why we need a strong union, so the change happens with us and not to us. I'd push the branch for a written deal on new machines on site.
S1.think: I'm nervous because pre-made forms would mean less cutting for us, and I'm slow with new tech. If the job changes a lot I'd be left behind.
S1.do: Asks the union branch to raise new equipment in talks with the contractor, aiming for notice, paid training and no layoffs without a deal. Keeps her savings untouched and sticks to the hand work she knows.
S1.feel: Uneasy, with a knot in her stomach, watching the site manager's face each morning.
S1.quote: I freeze when someone hands me a tablet and says it's simple.
S1.fieldNote: She knows her resistance to new tools is a weak spot and says so plainly. Her answer to that is collective protection rather than learning, and she points to her partner's union as proof it can work. She leaves the new kit to younger workers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be angry and I'd say it loud. At work I'd say they've done this to us without asking, and online I'd be sharing every petition going. I'd tell friends this is what happens when nobody regulates the people with the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd be finished as a carpenter. If a robot can build formwork and do it cheaper, the contractor won't keep six of us on out of kindness. I've got about three months saved, and two years isn't long enough for me to become anything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd stop the extras: the gym, the takeaways on Friday, the trip to see my sister. I'd move every spare penny into savings to try to get to six months. I'd be at every union meeting and every rally, and I'd vote and campaign for whoever promised a wage guarantee or a tax on the robot owners.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the floor's going. I'd be lying awake next to Jonah doing the sums in my head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Jonah actually talk about that first night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether his job goes too, because a bus is easier to automate than a building site. If we both go, we can't keep the flat on Mill Lane, and we'd probably end up back at my mum's. I'd hate that, but I'd rather that than debt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dev, straight away. He's four years off his pension and he can't start again at 61. Me, I'm young enough to scrub floors if I have to, but he's given his knees to this trade.

S2.say: I'd say they've done this to us without asking, and I'd share every petition going. I'd tell friends this is what happens when no one regulates the people with the money.
S2.think: I think I'd be finished as a carpenter, because the contractor won't keep six of us on out of kindness. Three months saved and two years isn't enough for me to become something else.
S2.do: Cuts the gym, Friday takeaways and a family trip, and pushes all spare money into savings to reach six months. Goes to every union meeting and rally, and votes and campaigns for a wage guarantee or a tax on robot owners.
S2.feel: Like the floor is going. She'd lie awake doing the sums.
S2.quote: Me, I'm young enough to scrub floors if I have to, but he's given his knees to this trade.
S2.fieldNote: The two-year version takes away the thing she relies on, which is time for the union to win something. She thinks first about her older workmate and her partner's job, not herself. Her plans are about cutting back and campaigning, not retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a few years, so let's use them to get rules in place before the robots turn up. At work I'd be the one handing out leaflets in the cabin. Online I'd share stuff about countries that are protecting workers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is better than two, but I still don't see myself changing trades. I'd be 32 by then, and I'd probably still be hoping the union wins enough that the robots need a person beside them. It's not much of a plan, but it's mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and save hard, maybe three hundred a month instead of two, to get to six months by the time it lands. I'd put my name forward to be a union rep on site so I'm in the room when they talk about machines. I'd also keep an eye on the politics and vote for whoever's serious about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tense, but I can breathe. It's like knowing there's a big pour on Friday, you can plan for it, but it's still coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't change trades even with five years. Why not use the time to retrain?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I don't trust the courses. They'd send me on some six-week coding thing, and I'd be the worst one in the room. I'd rather spend those years making sure people like me aren't just thrown out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the extra savings once it arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep it as a cushion so I'm not taking the first rubbish job going. If I've got six months, I can wait for something decent. That's the whole point of saving, for me.

S3.say: I'd say we have a few years, so let's get rules in place before the robots turn up. I'd hand out leaflets in the site cabin and share news about countries that protect workers.
S3.think: Five years is better than two, but I still don't see myself changing trades. I'd be hoping the union wins enough that robots need a person beside them.
S3.do: Raises her savings to about three hundred a month, aiming for six months by the time AGI arrives. Puts herself forward as union rep on site and votes for whoever takes it seriously.
S3.feel: Tense but able to breathe, like knowing a big pour is booked for Friday.
S3.quote: They'd send me on some six-week coding thing, and I'd be the worst one in the room.
S3.fieldNote: Extra time lowers her alarm but doesn't change her strategy. She'd use the years to organise and save, not to learn something new, and she's honest that this is because she doubts herself. Becoming a rep is the biggest step she names.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years I'd say we've got no excuse, this time the government and the bosses can plan properly. I'd say it at branch meetings and I'd say it to anyone at the pub. I'd want a proper plan for trades, not just for office workers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd still be worried, because ten years has a way of disappearing. I've been saying I'll do my scaffold ticket for two years and haven't, so I know what I'm like. I'd probably drift along until about year seven and then panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd do what I always do: keep working, keep saving, keep going to the union. I'd probably wait and see how fast the robots actually get good before doing anything bigger. If the union ran a course that was in work hours and with people I know, I might do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried in a slow way. It's not panic, it's a thing in the back of my head every time I see an advert for some new machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd drift until year seven. What would wake you up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing one on a site near me, properly working, not in a video. If I drove past the new estate on the ring road and saw a robot fixing shutters, that'd be it. Until then I'd probably keep telling myself it's years off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Jonah say about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd tell me to stop putting it off, like he does with the scaffold ticket. He's better at planning than me. He'd probably sign us both up for something and drag me along.

S4.say: With ten years I'd say there's no excuse, and the government and the bosses must plan properly. I'd want a proper plan for trades, not only office workers.
S4.think: I'd still worry, because ten years disappears and I put things off. I'd probably drift along until about year seven and then panic.
S4.do: Keeps working, saving and going to union meetings, and waits to see how fast robots really improve. Would take a course only if the union ran it in work hours with people she knows.
S4.feel: A slow, background worry that comes back whenever she sees a new machine advertised.
S4.quote: If I drove past the new estate on the ring road and saw a robot fixing shutters, that'd be it.
S4.fieldNote: Unusually, the longest timeline doesn't calm her, because she knows she tends to put things off. She expects to wait until she sees a working robot locally. Her partner comes up as the one who'd push her to act.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, no question, because there's no time for the union or anyone to do anything. What would help is a guarantee that if they bring robots in, workers get paid while they find something else, and that people like Dev can retire early without losing their pension. And training that doesn't make you feel stupid.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about women on site, and it matters. It took me years to get taken seriously on a gang, and I'd be gutted to lose that just as I've got there. If the jobs shrink, I don't want to be last in, first out because of who I am.

headlineQuote: I keep everything in a paper notebook with a pencil, and when the site moved sign-in to a tablet I was the last one to get used to it.
portrait: Esther Baker is a 27-year-old formwork carpenter on a hospital extension who keeps her life in a paper notebook and goes to her union branch every month. She lives with her partner Jonah, a bus driver, and has about three months saved. She is calm if AI stays hype, uneasy with steady change, and alarmed by AGI in two years, when she thinks she'd be finished as a carpenter. More time lowers her fear only a little, because she knows she puts things off and doesn't trust herself to retrain. Her answer every time is the union, savings and politics, and she worries first about her older workmate Dev.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because there'd be no time for the union or anyone else to act before the work disappears.
whatWouldHelp: Pay guaranteed while displaced workers find something else, early retirement without pension loss for older workers like Dev, and training that doesn't make people feel stupid.
